What is C# and what is the .NET Framework?
questions.a: C# is a modern, object-oriented, type-safe programming language developed by Microsoft. The .NET Framework is a software development framework that provides a controlled programming environment to develop, run, and execute C# applications. It includes the Common Language Runtime (CLR) for execution and the Base Class Library (BCL) for pre-written code functionality.
p: .NET is the execution environment and library.
CLR executes code and manages memory.

questions.q: What are the core OOPs principles in C#?
questions.a: Object-Oriented Programming in C# relies on four main pillars: Encapsulation (hiding internal state using access modifiers), Inheritance (reusing code by deriving new classes from existing ones), Polymorphism (performing a single action in different forms using method overloading or overriding), and Abstraction (hiding complex implementation details and showing only essential features).

questions.q: Explain the difference between Value Types and Reference Types.
questions.a: Value types store data directly in the stack (e.g., int, bool, struct) and hold their own copy of data. Reference types store a reference to the memory address where the data is stored on the heap (e.g., string, class, array). When you copy a value type, you copy the value. When you copy a reference type, you only copy the memory address reference.
p: Value types hold actual data; reference types hold pointers.

questions.q: What is the difference between string and StringBuilder?
questions.a: The string class is immutable, meaning every time you modify a string (like concatenation), a new object is created in memory, which can impact performance. StringBuilder is mutable, meaning it can be modified without creating new objects, making it much more efficient for heavy string manipulation and concatenation loops.
p: Use StringBuilder for heavy string concatenation.

questions.q: What are access modifiers in C# and what are the main types?
questions.a: Access modifiers are keywords used to set the visibility or accessibility of classes, methods, and other members. The primary types in C# are: Public (accessible from anywhere), Private (accessible only within the same class), Protected (accessible within the same class and derived classes), Internal (accessible only within the same assembly), and Protected Internal.
p: Private: Accessible inside the class only.
Protected: Accessible in class and subclasses.
Internal: Accessible within the same project.

questions.q: What are the four fundamental principles of Object-Oriented Programming?
questions.a: The four fundamental principles are Encapsulation (bundling data and methods together while hiding internal state), Inheritance (reusing code by deriving new classes from existing ones), Polymorphism (allowing objects to be treated as instances of their parent class, enabling multiple forms), and Abstraction (hiding complex implementation details and showing only essential features).
p: Encapsulation: Hiding data using access modifiers (private, public).
Inheritance: Reusing code via parent-child class relationships.
Polymorphism: Using a single interface for different data types.
Abstraction: Hiding complexity with abstract classes and interfaces.

questions.q: What is the difference between string and StringBuilder in C#?
questions.a: In C#, strings are immutable, meaning every time you modify a string, a new object is created in memory, which can hurt performance during heavy manipulation. StringBuilder is mutable, meaning it can be modified in place without creating new objects, making it much more efficient for frequent concatenation or changes.
p: String is immutable (cannot be changed once created).
StringBuilder is mutable (can be modified in place).
Use StringBuilder for loops or heavy string manipulations.

questions.q: What is the difference between value types and reference types in C#?
questions.a: Value types hold their actual data directly in the stack (e.g., int, bool, structs). Reference types store a reference or memory address to the actual data located on the heap (e.g., class, string, array). When passing value types, a copy is made; when passing reference types, only the memory address is copied.
p: Value types store data directly and live on the stack.
Reference types store memory addresses and live on the heap.
Common value types: int, float, struct, char.
Common reference types: string, class, array, object.

questions.q: What is a try-catch block and how does exception handling work?
questions.a: A try-catch block is used to handle runtime errors gracefully in C#. The 'try' block contains code that might throw an exception. If an error occurs, execution jumps to the 'catch' block, preventing the application from crashing. An optional 'finally' block can be added to execute cleanup code regardless of whether an exception occurred.
p: Try block: Contains risky code that might throw an error.
Catch block: Handles the exception if one occurs.
Finally block: Always executes for cleanup (e.g., closing files).
Prevents application crashes and manages errors gracefully.

questions.q: What is the difference between Value Types and Reference Types?
questions.a: Value types store their actual data directly in the stack, while reference types store a reference (or pointer) on the stack that points to the actual data located on the heap. Examples of value types include int, bool, and structs. Examples of reference types include string, arrays, and classes. When you copy a value type, you create an independent duplicate of the data. When you copy a reference type, you only copy the memory address, meaning both variables point to the exact same object in memory.
p: Value types store data in the stack; reference types store data in the heap.
Value types hold the actual value; reference types hold a memory address.
Copying a value type duplicates the data; copying a reference type duplicates the pointer.

What is Django?
questions.a: Django is a high-level Python web framework that encourages rapid development and clean, pragmatic design. It follows the 'batteries-included' philosophy, meaning it comes with built-in features like an administrative interface, authentication, ORM, and form handling, allowing developers to focus on writing their app without needing to reinvent the wheel.
p: Encourages rapid development and clean design

questions.q: What is the MVT architectural pattern in Django?
questions.a: MVT stands for Model-View-Template. The Model handles data and database interactions via the ORM. The Template handles the user interface and presentation layer using HTML and Django Template Language. The View acts as the bridge, receiving HTTP requests, querying the Model for data, and returning an HTTP response rendered through the Template.
p: Model: Handles database data and ORM
View: Processes business logic and connects Model with Template
Template: Manages user interface and HTML presentation

questions.q: What is the difference between Django's MVT and the traditional MVC pattern?
questions.a: In traditional MVC (Model-View-Controller), the Controller handles user input and business logic, while the View displays the data. In Django's MVT, the framework itself acts as the Controller handling the request/response cycle, the View corresponds to the Controller's logic handling the request, and the Template handles the presentation layer.
p: MVC uses Controller for logic, Django uses View for logic
Django handles the Controller role internally
MVT View acts like an MVC Controller

questions.q: What is the role of the Model in Django MVT?
questions.a: The Model is a Python class that subclasses `models.Model` and represents a database table or collection. It defines the data structure, fields, and behaviors of your data. Django uses the Model to interact with the database via its Object-Relational Mapper (ORM), allowing developers to write database queries in Python instead of SQL.
p: Represents database tables as Python classes
Interacts with databases using Django ORM

questions.q: What is Inheritance in Django models and what are its types?
questions.a: Inheritance allows child models to inherit fields and behaviors from parent models. Django provides three types: Abstract base classes (for shared fields without a separate database table), Multi-table inheritance (where each model has its own table linked by a OneToOneField), and Proxy models (to modify Python-level behavior without changing the database schema).
p: Abstract base classes share fields via Meta: abstract = True.
Multi-table inheritance creates a database table for every model in the hierarchy.
Proxy models change Python behavior without altering the database.

questions.q: How is Encapsulation used in Django models?
questions.a: Encapsulation bundles data (fields) and the methods that operate on that data within a single class (the Model). Django models hide the complex underlying SQL queries and database interactions, exposing a clean Python API like save(), delete(), or custom model methods to interact with the database securely.
p: Combines data fields and business logic inside the model class.
Hides complex SQL queries behind simple Python methods.
Protects data integrity by restricting direct database access.

questions.q: What is Polymorphism in the context of Django models?
questions.a: Polymorphism allows different model classes to be treated through a common interface. While standard Django ORM queries return instances of specific classes, method overriding allows child models to redefine parent methods (like __str__ or clean()) to execute model-specific behavior when called dynamically.
p: Enables different models to respond to the same method call differently.
Achieved via method overriding in inherited models.
Standardizes interactions across diverse database entities.

questions.q: How does Abstraction apply to Django models?
questions.a: Abstraction hides complex database mechanics and platform-specific SQL syntax behind high-level Python abstractions. Developers define models using Python classes and field types (CharField, IntegerField), and Django automatically translates these into optimized SQL queries for databases like PostgreSQL, MySQL, or SQLite.
p: Hides raw SQL complexity from the developer.
Uses Python classes and attributes to represent database tables and columns.

questions.q: What is the difference between Django's save() and update() methods?
questions.a: The `save()` method operates on a single model instance, triggers model signals (`pre_save`, `post_save`), and executes Python code for every field. In contrast, the `update()` method performs a bulk SQL update on a QuerySet directly in the database without fetching objects into memory, bypassing signals and custom save logic.
p: save() works on single instances; update() works on QuerySets.
save() triggers signals and executes Python code; update() does not.
update() is faster for bulk operations because it runs a single SQL query.

questions.q: What are the four main OOPs principles in Python?
questions.a: The four main Object-Oriented Programming principles are Inheritance, Polymorphism, Encapsulation, and Abstraction. Inheritance allows a class to inherit attributes and methods from another class. Polymorphism lets different classes share the same method name. Encapsulation restricts direct access to data using private/protected variables. Abstraction hides complex implementation details and shows only essential features.
p: Inheritance: Reusing code from parent classes.
Polymorphism: Using a unified interface for different data types.
Encapsulation: Hiding internal data and restricting access.
Abstraction: Hiding complex logic behind simple interfaces.

What is Express.js?
questions.a: Express.js is a minimal, fast, and unopinionated web application framework for Node.js. It provides a robust set of features for building single-page, multi-page, or hybrid web applications and RESTful APIs. It simplifies the underlying Node.js HTTP module, making routing and middleware management much easier and cleaner.
p: Simplifies HTTP request and response handling

questions.q: Why is Express.js used in web development?
questions.a: Express.js is used because it drastically reduces development time by providing pre-built methods and utilities for handling HTTP requests, routing, and middleware. It is unopinionated, meaning developers have complete freedom to structure their application and choose their database, making it extremely versatile for building lightweight APIs and scalable web servers.

questions.q: What is middleware in Express.js?
questions.a: Middleware functions are functions that have access to the request object (req), the response object (res), and the next middleware function in the application's request-response cycle. They are used to execute code, modify request and response objects, end the request-response cycle, and call the next middleware in the stack.
p: Has access to req, res, and next objects
Can modify request and response data
Executes sequentially in the request cycle
Used for logging, authentication, and parsing

questions.q: How do you handle routing in Express.js?
questions.a: Routing in Express refers to how an application's endpoints (URIs) respond to client requests. You define routes using methods of the Express app object that correspond to HTTP methods, such as app.get(), app.post(), app.put(), and app.delete(), passing a path and a callback function to handle the request.
p: Uses methods like app.get() and app.post()
Maps HTTP verbs to specific callback functions

questions.q: What is Express.js and how does it differ from vanilla Node.js?
questions.a: Express.js is a minimal and flexible Node.js web application framework that provides a robust set of features for building web and mobile applications. While vanilla Node.js requires writing extensive boilerplate code using the built-in 'http' module to handle routing, parsing, and server setup, Express simplifies this with a clean, built-in routing system, middleware support, and modular architecture, drastically reducing development time.
p: Built on top of Node.js HTTP module

questions.q: What is middleware in Express.js?
questions.a: Middleware functions are functions that have access to the request object (req), the response object (res), and the next middleware function in the application's request-response cycle. They can execute any code, make changes to the request and response objects, end the request-response cycle, and call the next middleware in the stack using 'next()'.
p: Has access to req, res, and next objects
Can modify request and response data
Executes sequentially in the request cycle
Must call next() or end the response

questions.q: How do you handle routing in Express.js compared to vanilla Node.js?
questions.a: In vanilla Node.js, you must manually parse the URL using the 'url' module and check request methods using conditional statements (if/else or switch) on the 'req.url' string. Express.js provides a dedicated routing mechanism using methods corresponding to HTTP verbs (like app.get() and app.post()) that match paths and HTTP methods automatically, making URL handling much cleaner.
p: Uses HTTP method functions like app.get()
Supports route parameters and query strings easily
Cleaner code than vanilla switch statements

questions.q: How is error handling managed in Express.js?
questions.a: Express.js provides built-in error-handling middleware that takes four arguments instead of three: (err, req, res, next). When you pass an error to the 'next()' function inside any middleware or route handler, Express skips all regular middleware and jumps straight to the nearest error-handling middleware function, allowing centralized management of errors.
p: Uses specialized middleware with four arguments
Triggered by passing an error to next(err)

questions.q: What is Express.js middleware and why do we need it for parsing request bodies?
questions.a: Middleware functions are functions that have access to the request object (req), the response object (res), and the next middleware function in the application's request-response cycle. We need body-parser or built-in Express middleware because raw HTTP requests arrive as streams of data. Middleware intercepts these streams, parses the JSON or URL-encoded data, and attaches the resulting JavaScript object to req.body for easy access in our route handlers.
p: Functions with access to req, res, and next
Converts raw HTTP data streams into usable formats
Attaches parsed data directly to req.body

questions.q: What is the difference between express.json() and express.urlencoded()?
questions.a: express.json() is a built-in middleware function in Express that parses incoming requests with JSON payloads and is based on body-parser. It populates req.body with a JavaScript object. On the other hand, express.urlencoded() parses incoming requests with URL-encoded payloads, typically sent by HTML form submissions. It allows parsing rich objects and arrays encoded in the URL-encoded format, using the 'qs' library or the 'querystring' library based on configuration.
p: express.json() parses JSON formatted request bodies
express.urlencoded() parses HTML form submission data
Both attach their parsed results to req.body

What is Flask and why is it called a micro-framework?
questions.a: Flask is a lightweight Python web framework classified as a 'micro-framework' because it does not require particular tools or libraries. It keeps the core simple yet extensible, giving developers the freedom to choose their preferred databases, form validation libraries, and tools without enforcing a specific project structure.

questions.q: What are the core features of Flask?
questions.a: Flask's core features include a built-in development server and fast debugger, integrated support for unit testing, RESTful request dispatching, Jinja2 templating, and secure cookie support. It relies on Werkzeug for WSGI toolkit functionality and uses blueprints for organizing application components.
p: Support for Blueprints to organize code

questions.q: Explain the difference between Flask and Django.
questions.a: Flask is a micro-framework that provides minimal tools, allowing developers to pick their own libraries and architecture. Django is a 'batteries-included' framework that comes with a built-in ORM, admin panel, authentication system, and strict project structure, making Flask better for small apps and APIs, and Django better for large monolithic applications.
p: Flask is minimal; Django is all-inclusive
Flask lets you choose components; Django provides them
Flask is ideal for microservices and APIs

questions.q: What is routing in Flask?
questions.a: Routing in Flask refers to binding a URL to a specific Python function using the '@app.route()' decorator. This tells the application what URL should trigger our function and handles incoming HTTP requests, mapping them to the corresponding view function which returns a response.

questions.q: What is a route in Flask and how do you define it?
questions.a: A route in Flask maps a URL pattern to a Python function using the `@app.route()` decorator. When a user visits that URL, Flask executes the decorated function—called a view function—and sends its return value back to the browser as the HTTP response.
p: The function immediately below is the view function
The function return value is sent to the client browser

questions.q: What is the difference between a route and a view function?
questions.a: A route is the URL endpoint (like '/about') defined by the `@app.route` decorator, while the view function is the actual Python function that executes the logic and generates the response when that URL is accessed.
p: View function = Python code that runs for that URL
Route connects the URL to the view function

questions.q: How do you pass variables in Flask routes?
questions.a: You pass variables in Flask routes by enclosing variable names in angle brackets '<variable_name>' inside the route decorator string. This variable is then passed as an argument to the corresponding view function.
p: Variable name in route must match function parameter
Flask automatically passes the value to the function

questions.q: What data types can be passed in Flask route parameters and how do you specify them?
questions.a: Flask routes support string (default), int, float, path, and uuid data types. You specify them in the route decorator using the syntax '<converter:variable_name>', which ensures the URL parameter is converted to the correct Python type before reaching the view function.
p: Supports int, float, path, and uuid

questions.q: What is the difference between request.args and request.form in Flask?
questions.a: In Flask, request.args is used to access URL query parameters (sent via GET method, visible in the URL), while request.form is used to access form data submitted in the request body (sent via POST method, hidden from the URL). Both return ImmutableMultiDict objects.
p: request.form handles HTTP POST body data.

Inheritance: Reusing code from parent classes.
Polymorphism: Same interface for different types.

How does Tiered Compilation manage the transition between C1 and C2 compilers, and what triggers the compilation thresholds?
questions.a: Tiered compilation uses 5 levels. Level 0 is interpreted. Levels 1-3 use C1 (Client Compiler) with varying profiling (Invocation and Backedge counters). Level 4 uses C2 (Server Compiler). When method invocation or loop iteration counters exceed flags like -XX:CompileThreshold, the VM queues the method for compilation. Level 3 fully profiles code feeding statistics to C2 for aggressive optimizations like escape analysis and devirtualization.
p: Level 0 (Interpreter) to Level 3 (C1 with full profiling)
Invocation and Backedge counters trigger compilation queues
Level 4 (C2) applies heavy optimizations using C1 profiling data

questions.q: Explain On-Stack Replacement (OSR). When does the JVM trigger it, and what are the mechanics of replacing an active frame?
questions.a: OSR compiles a method while it is actively executing inside a long-running loop, bypassing standard method entry. It triggers when a backedge counter exceeds the OSR threshold before the method itself meets invocation criteria. The JVM allocates a new compiled stack frame, maps local variables and operand stack from the interpreted frame to the compiled frame layout, and seamlessly transfers execution mid-method.
p: Triggers on long-running loops via Backedge counters
Compiles method mid-execution without waiting for return
Reconstructs stack frames, mapping interpreter locals to compiled registers

questions.q: What happens during JIT deoptimization (Deopt), and what are the performance implications of frequent trap occurrences?
questions.a: Deoptimization occurs when a speculative JIT optimization (like an assumed class hierarchy) is invalidated by runtime events (e.g., loading a subclass). The JVM safely unwinds the compiled frame, recreates precise interpreter frames on the stack, and resumes execution in the interpreter. Frequent deopts cause severe performance degradation due to CPU overhead in frame remapping and thrashing the JIT compilation queue with recompilations.
p: Triggered when speculative assumptions fail at runtime
Unwinds compiled stack frames back to interpreter frames
Frequent traps cause CPU churn and severe performance degradation

questions.q: How do Code Cache fragmentation and sweeper mechanics impact long-running microservices under heavy JIT load?
questions.a: The Code Cache stores compiled native methods. As classes load and deoptimizations occur, dead or invalidated methods accumulate, causing fragmentation. The Code Cache sweeper periodically scans and reclaims memory. If the cache fills up (-XX:ReservedCodeCacheSize), JIT compilers stop compiling new methods, forcing the JVM into pure interpretation. Mitigation involves tuning cache sizes and monitoring sweeper threads.
p: Stores compiled native code with a fixed maximum size
Sweeper thread reclaims memory from dead or deoptimized methods
A full code cache disables JIT, reverting execution to the interpreter

questions.q: Explain how ZGC utilizes Colored Pointers and Load Barriers to achieve sub-millisecond pauses during concurrent relocation.
questions.a: ZGC encodes metadata—such as Finalizable, Remapped, MarkLive0, and MarkLive1—directly into the upper bits of 64-bit object references. Because pointers themselves carry object state, a Load Barrier intercepts reference reads on the application thread. If the barrier detects a stale pointer (not yet remapped), it transparently resolves the forwarding table, updates the reference, and returns the correct address. This eliminates Stop-The-World pause scaling relative to heap size.
p: Colored pointers store GC metadata in reference bits.
Load barriers intercept reads to lazily fix stale pointers.
Forwarding tables track moved objects concurrently.
Pause times remain decoupled from heap size.

questions.q: How does G1 handle Humongous Objects, and what are the performance implications of allocating objects larger than half a region?
questions.a: G1 allocates objects exceeding 50% of a standard region size into contiguous 'Humongous Regions' within the Tenured generation. These objects bypass Eden and Survivor spaces entirely. They are only collected during a Mixed GC or a full GC cycle, often triggering premature Concurrent Mark cycles. Because they are not moved during compaction, they cause severe internal fragmentation and can abruptly elevate memory pressure, leading to evacuation failures.
p: Humongous allocations span contiguous regions in Tenured space.
They bypass standard generational aging completely.
Collected only during mixed or full GC, risking fragmentation.
Frequent humongous allocations trigger premature GC cycles.

questions.q: Compare the mechanics of Shenandoah's Brooks Pointers versus ZGC's Colored Pointers. What are the trade-offs?
questions.a: Shenandoah uses Brooks Pointers—an extra word prefix embedded directly inside the object header that points to the object itself (or its forwarded copy). During compaction, threads update this pointer atomically. While this works on 32-bit and 64-bit architectures without specialized OS support, it increases object header overhead and causes cache-line bouncing. ZGC's Colored Pointers avoid object header bloat and cache contention by storing metadata in the reference, but they require 64-bit architectures and virtual memory trickery.
p: Brooks pointers add an extra word inside the object header.
Colored pointers store metadata directly in the reference bits.
Brooks pointers cause cache-line bouncing under high contention.
Colored pointers require 64-bit architectures and OS-level mapping.

questions.q: During a production incident, you observe frequent G1 evacuation failures ('To-space exhausted'). How do you diagnose and tune for this?
questions.a: An evacuation failure occurs when G1 lacks free regions to copy surviving objects into during young or mixed collections, forcing a costly Full GC. Diagnose via GC logs looking for 'To-space exhausted' and high survivor occupancy. Tune by increasing heap size, increasing region size (-XX:G1HeapRegionSize) to accommodate larger objects, widening the survivor space ratio, starting the concurrent marking cycle earlier (-XX:InitiatingHeapOccupancyPercent), or increasing `-XX:G1ReservePercent` to maintain a safety buffer.
p: Caused by lack of free regions during object evacuation.
Triggers expensive Stop-The-World Full GC fallback.
Mitigate by lowering IHOP and increasing reserve percentage.
Adjust region size to prevent premature fragmentation.

questions.q: How do StoreLoad, StoreStore, LoadLoad, and LoadStore memory barriers map to x86 and ARM architectures, and what is the cost of a full fence?
questions.a: On x86, loads and stores are strictly ordered except for StoreLoad (handled via locked instructions or `mfence`). ARM is weakly ordered, requiring explicit barrier instructions (`dmb`, `dsb`, `isb`) for all four types. A full fence stalls the CPU pipeline, flushing store buffers, destroying instruction-level parallelism, and heavily degrading multi-core throughput.
p: x86 enforces TSO implicitly, needing barriers mainly for StoreLoad.
ARM requires explicit barriers for almost all combinations.
Full fences flush store buffers and stall CPU execution pipelines.

questions.q: Explain how final fields provide initialization safety without synchronization, and why reordering is prohibited even if the reference escapes during construction.
questions.a: Final fields guarantee that once an object constructor finishes, the values assigned to its final fields are visible to all other threads without synchronization. The JMM inserts a StoreStore barrier between final field writes and the reference assignment, plus a LoadLoad barrier on architectures like Alpha, preventing the 'this' reference escape hazard.
p: StoreStore barrier guarantees final writes precede reference publication.
Provides immutability guarantees without explicit locking overhead.
Prevents reading stale default values on weakly-ordered architectures.

What is JPA (Java Persistence API)?
questions.a: JPA is a Java specification for managing relational data in applications. It provides an ORM layer, mapping Java objects to database tables. JPA defines a standard for accessing, persisting, and managing data between Java objects and a relational database.

questions.q: What problem does JPA solve?
questions.a: JPA addresses the object-relational impedance mismatch. It simplifies database interactions by allowing developers to work with Java objects instead of writing SQL. This reduces boilerplate code, improves code readability, and enhances developer productivity by abstracting database complexities.

questions.q: Explain the difference between JPA and Hibernate.
questions.a: JPA is a specification, while Hibernate is an implementation of that specification. JPA defines the standard, and Hibernate is a concrete library that implements the JPA standard. Other JPA implementations include EclipseLink and Apache OpenJPA.

questions.q: What are the key components of JPA?
questions.a: Key components include the EntityManager (for managing persistence operations), EntityManagerFactory (for creating EntityManager instances), Persistence Unit (configuration for database connection), and JPA annotations (for mapping Java classes to database tables).

questions.q: What is the purpose of the `@Entity` annotation in JPA?
questions.a: The `@Entity` annotation marks a Java class as a persistent entity, meaning it represents a table in the database. Each instance of the class corresponds to a row in that table. It's a fundamental annotation for mapping Java objects to database tables using JPA.

questions.q: What is the role of the `EntityManager` in JPA?
questions.a: The `EntityManager` is the core interface for interacting with the persistence context. It's used to perform operations like persisting (saving), retrieving, updating, and deleting entities. It manages the lifecycle of entities and synchronizes changes with the database.

questions.q: What is the difference between an EntityManagerFactory and an EntityManager in JPA?
questions.a: The EntityManagerFactory is a factory for creating EntityManager instances. It's heavyweight and typically created once per application. The EntityManager is a lightweight, short-lived object that manages persistence operations (CRUD) on entities within a specific transaction. Multiple EntityManagers can be created from a single EntityManagerFactory.
p: Factory is heavyweight, Manager is lightweight.

questions.q: What is an EntityManager in JPA?
questions.a: An EntityManager is an interface in JPA that manages the persistence operations (CRUD - Create, Read, Update, Delete) on entity instances. It provides methods for persisting, merging, removing, and finding entities in the database. It operates within a transaction scope.

questions.q: What is an EntityManagerFactory in JPA?
questions.a: An EntityManagerFactory is a factory class in JPA used to create EntityManager instances. It is a heavyweight object that is typically created once per application or persistence unit. It encapsulates the configuration details needed to connect to the database.

questions.q: How do you create an EntityManager from an EntityManagerFactory?
questions.a: You create an EntityManager by calling the `createEntityManager()` method on an EntityManagerFactory instance. This method returns a new EntityManager instance that can be used to manage entities.

p: Model handles database and business logic.
View handles user interface and presentation.
Controller acts as the bridge between Model and View.

questions.q: How does Laravel implement the MVC pattern?
questions.a: Laravel implements MVC by routing incoming HTTP requests directly to Controllers. The Controller interacts with Eloquent Models to fetch or save data from the database. p: Controllers interact with Eloquent Models for data.
Views use Blade templates to display data to users.

questions.q: Explain the difference between 'public', 'private', and 'protected' keywords in PHP.

p: Protected: Accessible within class and subclasses
Private: Accessible only inside the defining class

Its primary use case is building fast, scalable network applications, APIs, and real-time services like chat applications.
p: Powered by Google Chrome's V8 engine
Used mainly for backend and API development

questions.q: How does Node.js work under the hood?
questions.a: Node.js works on a single-threaded event loop architecture using non-blocking I/O operations. When a request comes in, the single thread handles it. If there's a blocking operation like a database query or file read, Node delegates it to the libuv thread pool, freeing the main thread to handle other requests. Once complete, a callback is pushed to the event loop.
p: Uses libuv library to handle background tasks

questions.q: What is the Event Loop in Node.js?
questions.a: The Event Loop is the mechanism that allows Node.js to perform non-blocking I/O operations despite JavaScript being single-threaded. It continuously monitors the call stack and the callback queue. If the call stack is empty, it takes callback functions from the queue and pushes them to the stack for execution.
p: Continuously checks call stack and queues
Enables high concurrency on a single thread

questions.q: What is the difference between blocking and non-blocking code in Node.js?
questions.a: Blocking code executes synchronously, meaning Node.js must wait for the current task to finish completely before moving to the next line of code, which freezes the application. Non-blocking code executes asynchronously; tasks like file reads or network requests are handed off with a callback function, allowing Node.js to process other requests immediately.
p: Blocking is synchronous and freezes execution
Non-blocking is asynchronous and uses callbacks
Non-blocking improves application performance and throughput

questions.q: What is the V8 engine?

questions.q: What is a foreign key?

questions.q: Explain Encapsulation.

questions.q: What is Inheritance?

questions.q: What is Polymorphism?

questions.q: Explain Abstraction.

questions.q: What is the difference between method overloading and method overriding?

questions.q: What are stored procedures in PL/SQL?

questions.q: What are triggers in PL/SQL?

questions.q: What is exception handling in PL/SQL?

questions.q: Explain the key difference in execution between SQL and PL/SQL.

Abstraction: Hiding complexity and showing only essentials.

questions.q: What is the difference between private, protected, and public methods in Ruby?
questions.a: Public methods can be called by anyone; they form the public interface of the class. Protected methods can be invoked only by objects of the defining class or its subclasses. Private methods are strictly internal and can only be called implicitly on the current object; they cannot be called with an explicit receiver, not even on 'self'. In Ruby, methods defined below the 'private' or 'protected' keyword take on that visibility.
p: Protected: Accessible within the class hierarchy.
Private: Accessible only within the context of the current object without an explicit receiver.

questions.q: What are the basic data types in Ruby?
questions.a: Ruby is fully object-oriented, so everything is an object, including basic data types. Common data types include Numbers (Integer, Float), Strings, Booleans (TrueClass, FalseClass), Symbols, Arrays, and Hashes. Symbols are immutable, reusable identifiers often used as hash keys, while Strings are mutable sequences of characters.
p: Everything in Ruby is an object.
Numbers include both Integer and Float.

questions.q: How do you handle exceptions in Ruby?
questions.a: Exceptions in Ruby are handled using the 'begin', 'rescue', 'ensure', and 'end' blocks. Code that might raise an error is placed inside the 'begin' block. If an error occurs, execution jumps to the 'rescue' block where the exception can be caught and handled. The 'ensure' block contains code that always executes regardless of whether an exception occurred or not, commonly used for cleanup tasks like closing database connections.
p: Use 'rescue' to catch and handle errors.

questions.q: What is the difference between a Symbol and a String in Ruby?
questions.a: Strings are mutable objects used for readable text, and a new object is created in memory every time they are declared. Symbols are immutable, lightweight identifiers prefixed with a colon (:). Ruby only creates one copy of a symbol in memory throughout the application's lifecycle, making them much more memory-efficient and faster for comparisons, which is why they are frequently used as hash keys.
p: Strings are mutable; Symbols are immutable.
Strings allocate new memory each time; Symbols are reused (singleton objects).
Symbols are faster for comparisons and commonly used as hash keys.

questions.q: What are the four main Object-Oriented Programming (OOP) principles in Ruby?
questions.a: The four main OOP principles are Encapsulation, Inheritance, Polymorphism, and Abstraction. Encapsulation bundles data and methods within a class and restricts direct access. Inheritance allows a class to inherit behaviors from a parent class. Polymorphism lets different classes respond to the same method interface. Abstraction hides complex implementation details and exposes only the essential features.
p: Encapsulation: Bundling data and restricting access.
Inheritance: Reusing code through parent-child class relationships.
Polymorphism: Different objects responding to the same method call.

questions.q: What is Spring Boot?
questions.a: Spring Boot is a framework built on top of the Spring Framework that simplifies the creation of stand-alone, production-grade Spring based Applications. It favors convention over configuration, reducing the amount of boilerplate code required. It offers features like auto-configuration and embedded servers.

questions.q: What are the advantages of using Spring Boot?
questions.a: Spring Boot offers several advantages, including reduced development time, simplified configuration, embedded servers for easy deployment, and a wide range of starter dependencies that handle common application requirements. It promotes a more streamlined and efficient development process.

questions.q: What is auto-configuration in Spring Boot?
questions.a: Auto-configuration in Spring Boot automatically configures your application based on the dependencies you have added. It examines your classpath and configures beans accordingly, reducing the need for manual configuration. It intelligently sets up default configurations based on the project's dependencies.

questions.q: What are Spring Boot Starters?
questions.a: Spring Boot Starters are a set of convenient dependency descriptors that you can include in your application. Each starter bundles all the dependencies needed for a specific functionality, such as web development, data access, or security. They simplify dependency management and reduce the risk of version conflicts.

questions.q: How do you create a Spring Boot project?
questions.a: You can create a Spring Boot project using Spring Initializr (start.spring.io), which allows you to select the necessary dependencies and generate a basic project structure. Alternatively, you can use your IDE's built-in Spring Boot project creation tools or manually configure a Maven or Gradle project.

questions.q: What is an embedded server in Spring Boot?
questions.a: An embedded server is a web server that is packaged directly within your Spring Boot application. Spring Boot supports embedded Tomcat, Jetty, and Undertow servers. This eliminates the need to deploy your application to an external server, simplifying deployment and making it more portable.
p: Web server packaged within the application.

questions.q: What is Dependency Injection (DI)?
questions.a: Dependency Injection (DI) is a design pattern where an object receives its dependencies from an external source rather than creating them itself. This promotes loose coupling and makes code more testable and maintainable. Spring Boot heavily utilizes DI.

questions.q: What are the benefits of using Dependency Injection?
questions.a: DI offers several benefits, including reduced coupling between components, increased code reusability, improved testability (as dependencies can be easily mocked), and enhanced maintainability. It also promotes a more modular and organized codebase.

questions.q: How does Spring Boot implement Dependency Injection?
questions.a: Spring Boot implements DI through its Inversion of Control (IoC) container. The container manages the creation and wiring of dependencies. This is typically achieved using annotations like `@Autowired`, `@Component`, `@Service`, and `@Repository` to declare dependencies and components.

questions.q: What is the difference between Constructor Injection and Setter Injection?
questions.a: Constructor Injection provides dependencies through the class constructor, ensuring that the object is created with all required dependencies. Setter Injection provides dependencies through setter methods, allowing for optional dependencies. Constructor Injection is generally preferred for mandatory dependencies.
